key_points.point: The document highlights the potential for AI to act as a powerful research assistant that accelerates the information-gathering and synthesis phases of scholarly work. By automating time-intensive tasks, AI allows researchers to focus on higher-level inquiry and hypothesis testing. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of using AI to augment human productivity and expand the boundaries of what is possible in scientific discovery. The author notes, however, that current tools are primarily used for 'normal science' rather than revolutionary exploration.
key_points.verbatim: While these systems compile existing knowledge rather than generating novel insights, they speed up an important part of the research process by automating the time-intensive work of information gathering and initial synthesis.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'In addition to repeated encounters with the unusual...'

key_points.point: The author discusses the creation of interactive, AI-powered research environments that allow scholars to immerse themselves in historical data and discover latent connections. This approach frames AI as a 'cybernetic teammate' that enables rapid prototyping of digital humanities projects that previously required years of effort. From an accelerationist perspective, this demonstrates how AI lowers the barrier to entry for complex research, effectively democratizing the ability to perform high-level intellectual work. The author acknowledges that this is still an early-stage application of the technology.
key_points.verbatim: The historian Benjamin Breen has used AI coding tools to rapidly build interactive environments that combine cultural heritage collections and LLMs so that he and other scholars can immerse themselves an era or set of documents in a free-form, thought-provoking way.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'In addition to repeated encounters with the unusual...'

key_points.point: The document acknowledges the rapid acceleration of AI capabilities, noting that models are roughly three times as able as they were a year ago on comprehensive academic exams. This empirical observation supports the accelerationist belief in the predictable, rapid growth of AI intelligence. The author uses this to contrast current performance with the limitations of AI in generating truly novel research questions. The caveat is that while capabilities grow, the 'normality' of the research output remains constrained by existing frameworks.
key_points.verbatim: The best LLMs had already surpassed me, and now, a year later, the latest models are roughly three times as able as they were a year ago on that same exam, still far from perfect but capable of producing accurate answers to very tough questions from the full range of academic disciplines.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'A year ago, with tongue firmly in cheek...'

key_points.point: The author envisions a future where AI systems are designed to handle much larger context windows, allowing researchers to upload entire research briefs rather than just keywords. This desire for AI to act as a comprehensive repository and processor of human knowledge aligns with the accelerationist goal of creating AI that can manage and synthesize vast amounts of information. The author suggests this could move AI beyond simple summarization toward more active, exploratory research support. The limitation is that current interfaces are still too focused on narrow, answer-oriented tasks.
key_points.verbatim: All of these services could take advantage of the much larger context windows — the length of input text — that today's LLMs can handle. For example, it would be useful to have a scholar upload a research brief, rather than typing in mere keywords, when beginning a search and discovery process.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'Kuhn’s famous answer to where new questions...'

key_points.point: The document references a study in Nature that highlights a paradox: AI tools expand individual impact but contract the collective reach of science by focusing on data-rich areas. This concern about the long-term societal impact of AI on the direction of scientific progress is a core safetyist interest. The author uses this to argue that AI is currently automating established fields rather than exploring new ones, which could lead to a stagnation of scientific diversity. The document acknowledges this as a tension between personal advancement and collective progress.
key_points.verbatim: [The] adoption of AI in science presents what seems to be a paradox: an expansion of individual scientists’ impact but a contraction in collective science’s reach, as AI-augmented work moves collectively towards areas richest in data.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'The rapid acceleration, but overall normality...'

key_points.point: The author suggests that AI systems should be designed to 'surprise' scholars by surfacing items that wouldn't show up in standard searches, rather than always providing perfect alignment. This intention to introduce friction and prevent the narrowing of inquiry is a safetyist approach to maintaining human cognitive independence. By forcing researchers to encounter the unusual, the system avoids the risk of 'cognitive atrophy' or over-reliance on automated, biased search results. The author notes that this is a departure from current AI design, which favors summarization.
key_points.verbatim: But it might be worth surprising scholars from time to time rather than always giving them perfect alignment. This surprise could take the form of a sidebar of items that wouldn't show up in a standard Boolean search.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'Kuhn’s famous answer to where new questions...'

key_points.point: The document discusses the risk that AI tools might automate established fields and reduce follow-on engagement in less data-rich areas. This aligns with the safetyist concern regarding the 'intelligence displacement spiral,' where reliance on AI leads to a reduction in human exploration and cognitive engagement. The author warns that without intentional design to highlight the invisible or understudied, AI will simply reinforce existing biases in scientific research. The caveat is that this is a structural design issue, not an inherent limitation of the technology itself.
key_points.verbatim: With reduced follow-on engagement, AI tools seem to automate established fields rather than explore new ones, highlighting a tension between personal advancement and collective scientific progress.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'The rapid acceleration, but overall normality...'

key_points.point: The author emphasizes that AI models are currently 'answer-machines' that lack the curiosity or situational awareness to ask pointed questions about the nature of their own domains. This lack of self-understanding is a key safetyist concern, as it limits the ability of AI to act as a truly autonomous or collaborative agent. The author uses the example of AlphaFold to illustrate that even powerful AI is bounded by well-defined rules and cannot 'pause' to question its own purpose. The document acknowledges that this is a limitation of current popular forms of AI.
key_points.verbatim: AlphaFold is not going to pause one day, blank the screen of a startled biochemist, and ask pointed questions in a green phosphor font about the nature of proteins, which still have many strange and poorly understood functions.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'The rapid acceleration, but overall normality...'

key_points.point: The author argues that current AI models are structurally designed as 'answer-machines' that are poorly suited for the PhD-level work of formulating open-ended questions. This skepticism toward the 'intelligence' of AI is based on the observation that AI is designed to be on the 'A' side of Q&A, not the 'Q' side. From a skeptic perspective, this highlights the inherent design bias of current models toward providing easy answers rather than facilitating deep inquiry. The author acknowledges that AI can reverse this polarity briefly, but it is not its primary function.
key_points.verbatim: Structurally and interface-wise, Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are mostly answer-machines for our questions right now. Yes, they can ask us questions in response to our prompts, reversing the polarity briefly, but they are designed to be on the A side of Q&A.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'So the open-ended question I pose here is...'

key_points.point: The document frames AI progress as 'normal science'—the work of filling out existing models—rather than a revolutionary force. This aligns with the skeptic belief that AI will be slowly integrated into existing modes of knowledge work as a powerful tool, rather than fundamentally changing them. The author uses the term 'normal technology' to describe this incremental adoption. The caveat is that while AI is impressive, it is not currently capable of the kind of paradigm-shifting inquiry that defined the work of figures like Mandelbrot.
key_points.verbatim: (Note that AI as “normal science” is different from, but not entirely unrelated to, AI as “normal technology,” a parallel critique suggesting that AI, while an extremely powerful tool, will be slowly integrated into modes of knowledge work we already understand, rather than revolutionizing them.)
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'In short, AI progress in some areas of research...'

key_points.point: The author argues that the ability to formulate distinctive, uncommon, and open-ended questions is the hallmark of advanced research, and that AI's current focus on providing answers is a limitation. This skepticism toward AI-assisted research stems from the belief that the struggle to formulate questions is essential to the research process. By providing easy answers, AI may hinder the development of new ideas and interpretations. The author suggests that we should be wary of grading AI intelligence based on its ability to answer questions alone.
key_points.verbatim: If we are going to grade the “intelligence” of AI based on its ability to answer PhD-level questions, we are missing a critical point about PhD-level work: In advanced research what we value the most is not the ability to crank out airtight answers, but the ability to formulate distinctive, uncommon, and often openended questions.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'My point in that piece, however, was right there in the title...'

key_points.point: The author compares the current state of AI engagement to the early days of AOL, suggesting that we are in a 'comfortable, contained, and relatively inflexible' phase of a new digital world. This skeptical framing suggests that the current AI hype is a precursor to a more expansive, but not necessarily magical, future. The author emphasizes that human beings still have many ways to conceive new ideas without technology, reinforcing the idea that AI is just one tool among many. The document acknowledges that the Web eventually became a better environment for generating ideas, implying a similar potential for AI.
key_points.verbatim: We may very well look back on our first years of engagement with AI in forms like ChatGPT as we now look back on AOL before the flourishing of the World Wide Web — a comfortable, contained, and relatively inflexible introduction to a new digital world.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'We may very well look back on our first years...'

factual_claims.claim: The latest AI models are roughly three times as able as they were a year ago on comprehensive academic exams.
Benoît Mandelbrot's 1967 study 'How Long Is the Coast of Britain?' gave rise to an entirely new field in mathematics.
Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold can handle over 200 million protein structure predictions.

This suggests that AI's current integration into research may be inadvertently stifling the exploration of novel or understudied areas.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_label: Normal Science vs. Normal Technology Framing
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept provides a useful framework for distinguishing between AI as a tool for puzzle-solving within existing paradigms and AI as a standard, incrementally adopted technology.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Accelerationists would interpret this as a temporary phase where AI is being integrated into existing workflows before it eventually breaks through to create new, revolutionary paradigms.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Safetyists would use this to argue that we are currently in a 'normal science' phase that is prone to stagnation and bias, requiring active intervention to ensure AI is used for genuine exploration.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Skeptics would use this to validate their view that AI is not a magical, revolutionary force, but rather a standard, incrementally adopted tool that will not fundamentally change the nature of knowledge work.
